title: Applied Statistics I
subject: Statistics

cards.prompt: Define alternative hypothesis. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The set of parameter values or distributions contrasted with the null and aligned with the direction or difference the test is designed to detect.
required_concepts: The set of parameter values or distributions contrasted with the null and aligned with the direction or difference the test is designed to detect.
major_error_concepts: Choosing the alternative direction after seeing the sample estimate.

cards.prompt: Define analysis plan. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A pre-specified record of estimands, data exclusions, transformations, procedures, tails, error levels, sensitivity checks, and reporting rules.
required_concepts: A pre-specified record of estimands, data exclusions, transformations, procedures, tails, error levels, sensitivity checks, and reporting rules.
major_error_concepts: Writing the analysis plan after inspecting outcomes and presenting it as pre-specified.

cards.prompt: Give the endpoints of a basic bootstrap confidence interval and state what its quantiles represent.
cards.definition: Let theta_hat be the original estimate and q_p the p quantile of its bootstrap replicate distribution. The basic two-sided 1-alpha interval is [2 theta_hat-q_(1-alpha/2), 2 theta_hat-q_(alpha/2)]. It reflects bootstrap errors around the original estimate; its approximate coverage requires a suitable resampling scheme and validity conditions, not merely many replicates.
required_concepts: Use reflected endpoints 2 theta_hat minus the upper and lower bootstrap quantiles, in that order.
Quantiles are of bootstrap estimates, not raw observations.
Coverage relies on bootstrap validity rather than replicate count alone.
major_error_concepts: The basic interval is [2 theta_hat-q_(alpha/2),2 theta_hat-q_(1-alpha/2)], with the larger endpoint first.

cards.prompt: Define Type II error probability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For a specified alternative parameter value, beta is the probability that the test fails to reject the null.
required_concepts: For a specified alternative parameter value, beta is the probability that the test fails to reject the null.
major_error_concepts: Reporting one universal beta without specifying the alternative effect and design under which it is computed.

cards.prompt: Define bootstrap bias estimate. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The mean of the bootstrap estimator values minus the estimator value on the original sample, used as an approximation to estimator bias.
required_concepts: The mean of the bootstrap estimator values minus the estimator value on the original sample, used as an approximation to estimator bias.
major_error_concepts: Subtracting the unknown population parameter and calling the result bootstrap bias when the bootstrap calculation does not know that parameter.

cards.prompt: Define bootstrap distribution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The empirical distribution of an estimator recomputed across many bootstrap samples conditional on the observed data.
required_concepts: The empirical distribution of an estimator recomputed across many bootstrap samples conditional on the observed data.
major_error_concepts: Confusing the bootstrap distribution of a statistic with one bootstrap sample or with the original data distribution.

cards.prompt: Define bootstrap sample. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A pseudo-sample drawn with replacement from the empirical distribution, ordinarily with the same number of units as the original sample.
required_concepts: A pseudo-sample drawn with replacement from the empirical distribution, ordinarily with the same number of units as the original sample.
major_error_concepts: Sampling without replacement and calling the resulting permutation a nonparametric bootstrap sample.

cards.prompt: Define bootstrap standard error. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The sample standard deviation of the bootstrap distribution used to estimate the estimator's sampling standard error.
required_concepts: The sample standard deviation of the bootstrap distribution used to estimate the estimator's sampling standard error.
major_error_concepts: Computing standard deviation of all resampled observations and calling it the bootstrap standard error of the estimator.

cards.prompt: Define complete inferential report. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A result record combining the question and estimand, design and sample, estimate and effect scale, uncertainty, test decision when relevant, assumptions, sensitivity results, and limitations.
required_concepts: The report states the substantive question and the estimand.
The report describes the study design and sample.
The report gives the estimate and its effect scale.
The report gives uncertainty and, when relevant, the test decision.
The report states the assumptions and sensitivity results.
The report states important limitations.
major_error_concepts: Reporting only significant or not significant without estimate, interval, design, assumptions, effect importance, or selection context.

cards.prompt: Define confidence interval for a proportion. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** An interval procedure for a population proportion based on a sample proportion and a justified binomial or resampling approximation.
required_concepts: An interval procedure for a population proportion based on a sample proportion and a justified binomial or resampling approximation.
major_error_concepts: Reporting the sample proportion alone as a confidence interval or using an approximation outside its validity conditions without qualification.

cards.prompt: What does a frequentist confidence interval mean, and why is a realized interval not a posterior probability statement about a fixed parameter?
cards.definition: **Definition.** A statement about values compatible with the procedure and data together with its repeated-sampling coverage assumptions, not a posterior probability claim by default.
required_concepts: The interval reports parameter values compatible with the specified procedure and observed data.
Its interpretation depends on repeated-sampling coverage assumptions and is not a posterior probability claim by default.
major_error_concepts: Assigning the confidence level directly as the probability that the fixed parameter lies in the already observed interval.

cards.prompt: Define confidence interval. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The realized interval produced by a confidence procedure for an estimand from the observed sample.
required_concepts: The realized interval produced by a confidence procedure for an estimand from the observed sample.
major_error_concepts: Defining a confidence interval as the set containing the fixed frequentist parameter with a posterior probability equal to the confidence level.

cards.prompt: Define confidence level. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The nominal long-run coverage rate targeted by a confidence procedure, commonly written 1-alpha.
required_concepts: The nominal long-run coverage rate targeted by a confidence procedure, commonly written 1-alpha.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting the confidence level as the fraction of observed sample points inside the interval.

cards.prompt: Define coverage probability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The probability, under a specified parameter value and data-generating process, that the random interval produced by a procedure contains the estimand.
required_concepts: The probability, under a specified parameter value and data-generating process, that the random interval produced by a procedure contains the estimand.
major_error_concepts: Estimating coverage by asking what fraction of observations fall between one realized interval's endpoints.

cards.prompt: Define critical value. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A quantile of a reference distribution used to set an interval boundary or rejection threshold at a declared tail probability.
required_concepts: A quantile of a reference distribution used to set an interval boundary or rejection threshold at a declared tail probability.
major_error_concepts: Choosing a critical value from the observed estimate rather than the declared reference distribution and confidence or significance level.

cards.prompt: Define effect size. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A numerical magnitude of the population difference, association, or contrast relevant to the substantive question, expressed on a raw or standardized scale.
required_concepts: A numerical magnitude of the population difference, association, or contrast relevant to the substantive question, expressed on a raw or standardized scale.
major_error_concepts: Treating the p-value as an effect size or assuming a smaller p-value means a larger effect.

cards.prompt: Define empirical distribution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The distribution that assigns observed sample values their empirical frequencies, commonly mass one over n to each observation in an unweighted sample.
required_concepts: The distribution that assigns observed sample values their empirical frequencies, commonly mass one over n to each observation in an unweighted sample.
major_error_concepts: Treating the empirical distribution as the known true population distribution rather than a sample-based approximation.

cards.prompt: Define estimand. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The precisely defined population quantity the analysis intends to learn, including population, outcome, comparison, and aggregation choices.
required_concepts: The precisely defined population quantity the analysis intends to learn, including population, outcome, comparison, and aggregation choices.
major_error_concepts: Naming a metric such as accuracy without defining the target population, comparison, and aggregation and calling it a complete estimand.

cards.prompt: Define estimate. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The realized numerical value of an estimator after it is applied to the observed sample.
required_concepts: The realized numerical value of an estimator after it is applied to the observed sample.
major_error_concepts: Reporting an estimate as though it were the exact population parameter with no sampling uncertainty.

cards.prompt: Define estimated standard error. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A sample-based estimate of the unknown standard error, obtained analytically or by a valid resampling procedure.
required_concepts: A sample-based estimate of the unknown standard error, obtained analytically or by a valid resampling procedure.
major_error_concepts: Reporting an estimated standard error as exact while ignoring that it is computed from the realized sample and a procedure contract.

cards.prompt: Define Estimator bias. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The repeated-sampling expectation of an estimator minus the estimand it targets.
required_concepts: The repeated-sampling expectation of an estimator minus the estimand it targets.
major_error_concepts: Defining bias as the error in one realized estimate rather than an expectation across the sampling distribution.

cards.prompt: Define Estimator consistency. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The property that an estimator converges in probability to its estimand as sample size grows under specified assumptions.
required_concepts: The property that an estimator converges in probability to its estimand as sample size grows under specified assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Equating consistency with unbiasedness or with low error at one finite sample size.

cards.prompt: Define estimator mean squared error. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The expected squared difference between an estimator and its estimand, equal to estimator variance plus squared bias when the quantities exist.
required_concepts: The expected squared difference between an estimator and its estimand, equal to estimator variance plus squared bias when the quantities exist.
major_error_concepts: Adding bias rather than squared bias to variance when computing estimator MSE.

cards.prompt: Define Estimator variance. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The variance of an estimator under its sampling distribution, measuring repeated-sample dispersion around its own expectation.
required_concepts: The variance of an estimator under its sampling distribution, measuring repeated-sample dispersion around its own expectation.
major_error_concepts: Using variability of individual observations as though it were automatically the variance of the estimator.

cards.prompt: Define estimator. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A rule that maps a possible sample to a statistic used to estimate a specified estimand.
required_concepts: A rule that maps a possible sample to a statistic used to estimate a specified estimand.
major_error_concepts: Confusing the estimator rule across possible samples with the single numerical estimate it produced.

cards.prompt: Define exchangeability for permutation inference. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Under the tested null and design, the joint distribution is invariant to the label or assignment permutations used by the procedure.
required_concepts: Under the tested null and design, the joint distribution is invariant to the label or assignment permutations used by the procedure.
major_error_concepts: Assuming observations are exchangeable solely because they share the same marginal scale.

cards.term: fail to reject the null hypothesis
cards.prompt: Define fail to reject the null hypothesis. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Apply the test rule and find insufficient evidence for rejection at the declared level; this does not establish that the null is true or equivalent.
required_concepts: Apply the test rule and find insufficient evidence for rejection at the declared level; this does not establish that the null is true or equivalent.
major_error_concepts: Converting failure to reject into acceptance or proof of no effect without an equivalence or noninferiority procedure.

cards.prompt: Distinguish finite-sample versus asymptotic guarantee.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A finite-sample guarantee holds at specified sample sizes, whereas an asymptotic guarantee describes limiting behavior as sample size grows.
required_concepts: A finite-sample guarantee states a property for specified finite sample sizes.
An asymptotic guarantee states limiting behavior as the sample size tends to infinity.
An asymptotic approximation need not give the stated finite-sample guarantee at a particular sample size.
major_error_concepts: Treating an asymptotic approximation as an exact finite-sample theorem without checking sample size and assumptions.

cards.prompt: Define interval estimator. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A rule that maps a sample to lower and upper bounds intended to cover an estimand at a specified repeated-sampling rate.
required_concepts: A rule that maps a sample to lower and upper bounds intended to cover an estimand at a specified repeated-sampling rate.
major_error_concepts: Confusing the random interval-generating procedure with the fixed endpoints observed after sampling.

cards.prompt: Define confidence interval width. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The upper endpoint minus the lower endpoint, reflecting critical level, estimator uncertainty, sample size, and procedure choice.
required_concepts: The upper endpoint minus the lower endpoint, reflecting critical level, estimator uncertainty, sample size, and procedure choice.
major_error_concepts: Comparing widths from different estimands or confidence levels as though narrower always means a better procedure.

cards.prompt: Define margin of error. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The distance from a symmetric interval's point estimate to either endpoint, typically critical value times estimated standard error.
required_concepts: The distance from a symmetric interval's point estimate to either endpoint, typically critical value times estimated standard error.
major_error_concepts: Calling the full interval width the margin of error rather than twice the margin for a symmetric interval.

cards.prompt: Define model misspecification. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A mismatch between the assumed statistical model or dependence structure and the process that generated the data, potentially invalidating nominal inference.
required_concepts: A mismatch between the assumed statistical model or dependence structure and the process that generated the data, potentially invalidating nominal inference.
major_error_concepts: Restricting misspecification to non-normal histograms while ignoring dependence, measurement, sampling, and functional-form errors.

cards.prompt: Define nonparametric procedure. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A procedure that avoids fixing a finite-dimensional parametric family for the full data distribution, while still relying on sampling and structural assumptions.
required_concepts: A nonparametric procedure does not fix a finite-dimensional parametric family for the full data distribution.
The procedure still relies on a declared sampling model or sampling assumptions.
The procedure can still rely on structural assumptions specific to the method.
major_error_concepts: Describing nonparametric as assumption-free or automatically valid for dependent, biased, or tiny samples.

cards.prompt: Define null distribution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The sampling distribution of the test statistic when the null hypothesis and procedure assumptions hold.
required_concepts: The sampling distribution of the test statistic when the null hypothesis and procedure assumptions hold.
major_error_concepts: Using the empirical distribution of raw observations as the null distribution of the test statistic.

cards.prompt: Define null hypothesis. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The reference hypothesis whose compatibility with the data is assessed by the test procedure, often representing no effect or a boundary value.
required_concepts: The reference hypothesis whose compatibility with the data is assessed by the test procedure, often representing no effect or a boundary value.
major_error_concepts: Treating the null hypothesis as automatically true or as the probability model favored by the analyst.

cards.prompt: Define observation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The realized value or values recorded for an observational unit under a declared measurement process.
required_concepts: The realized value or values recorded for an observational unit under a declared measurement process.
major_error_concepts: Confusing the realized observation with the variable or with the entire observational unit.

cards.prompt: Define observational unit. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The entity on which variables are measured or from which one statistical record is generated under the study design.
required_concepts: The entity on which variables are measured or from which one statistical record is generated under the study design.
major_error_concepts: Assuming each row is an independent observational unit merely because the data file stores one row per measurement.

cards.prompt: Distinguish one-sided versus two-sided confidence interval.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A one-sided procedure provides only an upper or lower confidence bound, while a two-sided procedure provides both bounds with tail allocation matched to the question.
required_concepts: A one-sided confidence procedure reports only an upper bound or only a lower bound.
A two-sided confidence procedure reports both a lower bound and an upper bound.
The direction and tail allocation must be chosen to match the inferential question.
major_error_concepts: Switching from two-sided to one-sided reporting after seeing which direction the estimate moved.

cards.prompt: Distinguish one-sided versus two-sided test.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A one-sided test allocates rejection probability to a predeclared direction, while a two-sided test allocates it to departures in both directions.
required_concepts: A one-sided test places its rejection probability in one predeclared direction.
A two-sided test allows rejection for departures in both directions.
The direction chosen before inspecting the result determines how the rejection probability is allocated.
major_error_concepts: Halving a two-sided p-value after observing the favorable sign and calling it a predeclared one-sided test.

cards.prompt: What does outlier influence diagnose or distinguish?
cards.definition: **Definition.** The change in an estimator or conclusion attributable to an unusually positioned observation under a defined perturbation or deletion analysis.
required_concepts: The change in an estimator or conclusion attributable to an unusually positioned observation under a defined perturbation or deletion analysis.
major_error_concepts: Deleting an observation solely because it weakens significance and calling that objective outlier handling.

cards.prompt: What important conclusions cannot be drawn from a p-value alone?
cards.definition: **Definition.** A p-value does not by itself measure effect magnitude, practical importance, probability a hypothesis is true, or the full evidential strength of a study.
required_concepts: A p-value alone does not measure the magnitude of an effect.
A p-value alone does not establish the practical importance of an effect.
A p-value alone is not the probability that a hypothesis is true.
A p-value alone does not summarize the full evidential strength or quality of a study.
major_error_concepts: Using whether p crosses 0.05 as the sole basis for a scientific, deployment, or policy conclusion.

cards.prompt: Under the specified null model, what probability does a p-value report, and what does it not say about the probability that the null hypothesis is true?
cards.definition: **Definition.** Under the specified null model, a p-value is the probability of a test statistic at least as incompatible with the null as the observed statistic, using the declared tail rule. It is not the posterior probability that the null hypothesis is true given the data.
required_concepts: The p-value is computed under the specified null model using the declared tail rule.
It is the probability of a test statistic at least as incompatible with the null as the observed statistic.
It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true given the observed data.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting the p-value as the posterior probability that the null is true or that chance alone produced the data.

cards.prompt: Define paired confidence interval. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A confidence interval formed from within-pair contrasts so shared-unit variation is retained in the uncertainty calculation.
required_concepts: A confidence interval formed from within-pair contrasts so shared-unit variation is retained in the uncertainty calculation.
major_error_concepts: Using an independent-samples standard error for matched observations without modeling their pairing.

cards.prompt: Define paired observations. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Two measurements linked by the same unit or an explicit matching rule so their within-pair difference carries the comparison information.
required_concepts: Two measurements linked by the same unit or an explicit matching rule so their within-pair difference carries the comparison information.
major_error_concepts: Calling two samples paired solely because they have equal size without a unit-level or matching correspondence.

cards.prompt: Define paired resampling. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Resampling paired units or their within-pair contrasts together so the dependence defining the estimand is preserved.
required_concepts: Resampling paired units or their within-pair contrasts together so the dependence defining the estimand is preserved.
major_error_concepts: Independently resampling the members of each pair and claiming the paired covariance has been preserved.

cards.prompt: Give the percentile bootstrap interval endpoints and distinguish them from the basic interval.
cards.definition: For bootstrap estimates theta_hat*, let q_p be their p quantile. The percentile 1-alpha interval is [q_(alpha/2),q_(1-alpha/2)]. Unlike the basic interval, these endpoints are not reflected around theta_hat. They use the estimator distribution, not raw-data quantiles; coverage is approximate and depends on a valid bootstrap for the target and sampling design.
required_concepts: Use lower and upper bootstrap-estimate quantiles directly.
Do not reflect the endpoints as in the basic interval.
The bootstrap scheme and estimator must support the intended coverage approximation.
major_error_concepts: A percentile bootstrap mean interval consists of the alpha/2 and 1-alpha/2 quantiles of the original observations.

cards.prompt: Define permutation test. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A test that compares the observed statistic with its distribution over valid permutations under an exchangeability or randomization null.
required_concepts: A test that compares the observed statistic with its distribution over valid permutations under an exchangeability or randomization null.
major_error_concepts: Permuting labels that are not exchangeable under the null and treating the resulting p-value as valid.

cards.prompt: Define Point estimator. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** An estimator that returns a single numerical value for the estimand rather than a set or distribution of plausible values.
required_concepts: An estimator that returns a single numerical value for the estimand rather than a set or distribution of plausible values.
major_error_concepts: Calling a confidence interval a point estimator because it has a midpoint.

cards.prompt: Define population parameter. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A fixed but generally unknown numerical feature of the target population or data-generating process.
required_concepts: A fixed but generally unknown numerical feature of the target population or data-generating process.
major_error_concepts: Treating a population parameter as random merely because the analyst is uncertain about its value in a frequentist analysis.

cards.prompt: Define population. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The full set or data-generating domain of units about which the statistical conclusion is intended to speak.
required_concepts: The full set or data-generating domain of units about which the statistical conclusion is intended to speak.
major_error_concepts: Equating the observed dataset with the target population without a sampling or scope argument.

cards.prompt: Define power-based sample-size planning. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Choosing sample size to attain target power for a specified effect, alpha, variability, test, and allocation before data collection.
required_concepts: Choosing sample size to attain target power for a specified effect, alpha, variability, test, and allocation before data collection.
major_error_concepts: Choosing sample size from a generic rule while omitting the effect, variability, alpha, and target power assumptions.

cards.prompt: Define Power function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The test procedure's rejection probability as a function of the true parameter or effect value.
required_concepts: The test procedure's rejection probability as a function of the true parameter or effect value.
major_error_concepts: Treating power as a single property of a test independent of effect size and data-generating assumptions.

cards.prompt: Define practical significance. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The substantive importance of an effect relative to costs, risks, baselines, and decision thresholds, distinct from statistical significance.
required_concepts: The substantive importance of an effect relative to costs, risks, baselines, and decision thresholds, distinct from statistical significance.
major_error_concepts: Equating statistical rejection at alpha with operational or scientific importance.

cards.prompt: Define precision-based sample-size planning. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Choosing sample size so an interval or estimator attains a target margin of error under declared variability and coverage assumptions.
required_concepts: Choosing sample size so an interval or estimator attains a target margin of error under declared variability and coverage assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Calling a power calculation a precision calculation without translating the goal into interval width or estimation error.

cards.prompt: Define inferential procedure assumption. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A condition on sampling, assignment, measurement, dependence, distribution, or model needed for a procedure's stated operating guarantee.
required_concepts: A condition on sampling, assignment, measurement, dependence, distribution, or model needed for a procedure's stated operating guarantee.
major_error_concepts: Listing normality alone as if it were the only assumption behind every confidence interval or test.

cards.prompt: Define random sample. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A sample selected by a known random mechanism that assigns population or frame units declared inclusion probabilities.
required_concepts: A sample selected by a known random mechanism that assigns population or frame units declared inclusion probabilities.
major_error_concepts: Calling a sample random because its records appear unordered or because a software shuffle was applied after convenience selection.

cards.prompt: Define reject the null hypothesis. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Apply the test rule and conclude that the observed statistic falls in the rejection region, while retaining the possibility of Type I error.
required_concepts: Apply the test rule and conclude that the observed statistic falls in the rejection region, while retaining the possibility of Type I error.
major_error_concepts: Translating rejection into certainty that the alternative is true or that the effect is practically important.

cards.prompt: Define rejection region. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The set of test-statistic outcomes for which the predeclared test rejects the null, calibrated under the null distribution and significance level.
required_concepts: The set of test-statistic outcomes for which the predeclared test rejects the null, calibrated under the null distribution and significance level.
major_error_concepts: Drawing the rejection region around the observed statistic after the data are known.

cards.prompt: Define relative efficiency. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A comparison of two estimators' sampling variances or asymptotic variances for the same estimand under the same data-generating assumptions.
required_concepts: A comparison of two estimators' sampling variances or asymptotic variances for the same estimand under the same data-generating assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Calling an estimator more efficient because it runs faster computationally when the comparison concerns statistical variance.

cards.prompt: Define repeated-sampling thought experiment. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The conceptual repetition of the declared sampling and analysis procedure over new samples from the same data-generating conditions.
required_concepts: The conceptual repetition of the declared sampling and analysis procedure over new samples from the same data-generating conditions.
major_error_concepts: Repeating calculations on the same fixed sample without resampling and calling that the frequentist repeated-sampling experiment.

cards.prompt: Define sample representativeness. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The degree to which the sample supports inference to the target population for the estimand, given coverage, inclusion, measurement, and dependence mechanisms.
required_concepts: The degree to which the sample supports inference to the target population for the estimand, given coverage, inclusion, measurement, and dependence mechanisms.
major_error_concepts: Declaring a sample representative from visual similarity on a few marginals without an inclusion or transport argument.

cards.prompt: Define resampling method. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A computational procedure that repeatedly constructs pseudo-samples or rearrangements from observed data to approximate a sampling or null distribution.
required_concepts: A computational procedure that repeatedly constructs pseudo-samples or rearrangements from observed data to approximate a sampling or null distribution.
major_error_concepts: Calling repeated evaluation of the unchanged observed sample resampling.

cards.prompt: Define resampling Monte Carlo error. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Random numerical error from using a finite number of simulated resamples or permutations to approximate a resampling quantity.
required_concepts: Random numerical error from using a finite number of simulated resamples or permutations to approximate a resampling quantity.
major_error_concepts: Treating a finite-resample result as exact because the original dataset is fixed.

cards.prompt: Define robust statistical procedure. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A procedure whose performance or conclusion changes only modestly under specified departures, contamination, or influential observations.
required_concepts: A procedure whose performance or conclusion changes only modestly under specified departures, contamination, or influential observations.
major_error_concepts: Calling a procedure robust without specifying the perturbation class and performance quantity being protected.

cards.prompt: Define sample statistic. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A numerical function of the observed sample that contains no unknown population parameter.
required_concepts: A numerical function of the observed sample that contains no unknown population parameter.
major_error_concepts: Calling a formula a statistic when it still contains the unknown parameter it is meant to estimate.

cards.prompt: Define sample. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The finite collection of observed units or measurements used for the analysis, selected under a stated sampling mechanism.
required_concepts: The finite collection of observed units or measurements used for the analysis, selected under a stated sampling mechanism.
major_error_concepts: Calling every available record a random sample without specifying how inclusion occurred.

cards.prompt: Define sampling bias. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Systematic distortion of an estimator's target caused by the sample inclusion mechanism or frame differing from the intended population.
required_concepts: Systematic distortion of an estimator's target caused by the sample inclusion mechanism or frame differing from the intended population.
major_error_concepts: Treating a larger convenience sample as automatically unbiased even though its inclusion mechanism remains systematically selective.

cards.prompt: Define sampling distribution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The probability distribution of an estimator across repeated samples generated under the declared sampling process.
required_concepts: The probability distribution of an estimator across repeated samples generated under the declared sampling process.
major_error_concepts: Confusing the empirical distribution of observed values with the sampling distribution of a statistic.

cards.prompt: Define sampling frame. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The operational list or mechanism from which candidate population units can be selected for the sample.
required_concepts: The operational list or mechanism from which candidate population units can be selected for the sample.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a sampling frame covers the target population without checking excluded, duplicated, or unreachable units.

cards.prompt: Define selective reporting. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Reporting a data-dependent subset of analyses, outcomes, subgroups, or stopping times without disclosing the selection process.
required_concepts: Reporting a data-dependent subset of analyses, outcomes, subgroups, or stopping times without disclosing the selection process.
major_error_concepts: Treating undisclosed analysis selection as harmless because each reported p-value used standard software.

cards.prompt: What does sensitivity analysis diagnose or distinguish?
cards.definition: **Definition.** A structured recomputation under plausible alternative assumptions, exclusions, measurements, or procedures to assess conclusion stability.
required_concepts: A structured recomputation under plausible alternative assumptions, exclusions, measurements, or procedures to assess conclusion stability.
major_error_concepts: Trying many analyses and reporting only the favorable one while calling the hidden search sensitivity analysis.

cards.prompt: Define significance level. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A predeclared bound or target for the Type I error probability of a test procedure, conventionally denoted alpha.
required_concepts: A predeclared bound or target for the Type I error probability of a test procedure, conventionally denoted alpha.
major_error_concepts: Treating alpha as the observed p-value or selecting alpha after seeing the p-value.

cards.prompt: Distinguish simple versus composite hypothesis.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A simple hypothesis specifies one complete parameter or distribution value, whereas a composite hypothesis contains multiple possible values or distributions.
required_concepts: A simple hypothesis specifies one complete parameter value or one complete data-generating distribution.
A composite hypothesis permits multiple parameter values or multiple data-generating distributions.
The separating invariant is the number of fully specified distributions compatible with the hypothesis.
major_error_concepts: Calling a one-sided inequality hypothesis simple because its notation is short.

cards.prompt: Define smallest effect size of interest. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The smallest effect magnitude declared substantively meaningful for planning, interpretation, or equivalence decisions.
required_concepts: The smallest effect magnitude declared substantively meaningful for planning, interpretation, or equivalence decisions.
major_error_concepts: Defining the smallest interesting effect after observing the estimate so the study appears conclusive.

cards.prompt: Define standard error. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The standard deviation of an estimator's sampling distribution under the declared sampling process.
required_concepts: The standard deviation of an estimator's sampling distribution under the declared sampling process.
major_error_concepts: Confusing standard error of an estimator with standard deviation of the individual observations.

cards.prompt: Define statistical hypothesis. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A testable claim specifying a set of possible values or distributions for a population parameter or data-generating process.
required_concepts: A testable claim specifying a set of possible values or distributions for a population parameter or data-generating process.
major_error_concepts: Writing a vague scientific hope such as the model is better without translating it into a claim about a defined population quantity.

cards.prompt: Define statistical inquiry. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A disciplined process that connects a substantive question to a target population and estimand, data collection, an analysis procedure, uncertainty, and a qualified conclusion.
required_concepts: Statistical inquiry begins with a substantive question tied to a target population and estimand.
It uses a declared data-collection or study-design process.
It applies an analysis procedure suited to the question and data.
It quantifies relevant uncertainty.
It ends with a conclusion qualified by the design, assumptions, and evidence.
major_error_concepts: Treating data analysis as choosing a test after seeing the data without first defining the population, estimand, and collection process.

cards.prompt: Define statistical power. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For a specified alternative, the probability that the test rejects the null, equal to one minus beta for that alternative.
required_concepts: For a specified alternative, the probability that the test rejects the null, equal to one minus beta for that alternative.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting power as the posterior probability that a significant result is correct.

cards.prompt: State the classical two-sided t confidence interval for a mean and its exact normal-model assumptions.
cards.definition: For n≥2 iid observations from N(mu,sigma²) with unknown sigma>0, let xbar be the sample mean and s²=sum_i(X_i-xbar)²/(n-1). The two-sided 1-alpha interval is xbar ± t_(n-1,1-alpha/2) s/sqrt(n), for 0<alpha<1. It has exact normal-model coverage. Outside that model a t-based approximation needs its own justification; a sample-size slogan is not an exact theorem.
required_concepts: State xbar ± t_(n-1,1-alpha/2) s/sqrt(n).
Use sample variance with n-1 degrees of freedom and n≥2.
Exact coverage assumes iid normal observations with unknown positive variance.
major_error_concepts: The exact unknown-variance interval is xbar ±1.96s for every distribution and every sample size.

cards.prompt: Define test-confidence interval duality. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For aligned procedures, a two-sided level-alpha test rejects a parameter value exactly when that value lies outside the corresponding 1-alpha confidence interval.
required_concepts: The duality applies to aligned two-sided level-alpha tests and corresponding 1-alpha confidence intervals.
The test rejects a parameter value exactly when that value lies outside the corresponding interval.
major_error_concepts: Applying duality across procedures with different assumptions, tails, estimands, or standard-error calculations.

cards.prompt: Define a test statistic. Can a calibrated p-value itself be used as one?
cards.definition: A test statistic is a declared function of the observed data used to order evidence against a null, with its reference distribution or calibration specified under that null. It may be a raw statistic or a transformation, including a p-value. Reusing a p-value as a statistic does not make it a posterior null probability, and any selection or combination must receive the appropriate null calibration.
required_concepts: The statistic is a function of observed data with a declared null calibration and extremeness convention.
A transformation such as a calibrated p-value can itself serve as a statistic.
accepted_variants: A statistic is a data function; a continuous exact-null p-value is such a function with a Uniform(0,1) null law. It can be thresholded or transformed, but a combination or selected statistic requires its own valid calibration.
major_error_concepts: A p-value cannot be a statistic because statistics never depend on a reference distribution.

cards.prompt: Define Type I error. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Rejecting the null hypothesis when the null condition is in fact true; its procedure probability is controlled by alpha under assumptions.
required_concepts: Rejecting the null hypothesis when the null condition is in fact true; its procedure probability is controlled by alpha under assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Calling any incorrect scientific conclusion a Type I error without conditioning on a true null and a rejection decision.

cards.prompt: Define Type II error. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Failing to reject the null when a specified alternative condition is true.
required_concepts: Failing to reject the null when a specified alternative condition is true.
major_error_concepts: Calling every non-rejection a Type II error without knowing that a specified alternative is true.

cards.prompt: Define Unbiased estimator. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** An estimator whose repeated-sampling expectation equals its estimand under the stated model and sampling process.
required_concepts: An estimator whose repeated-sampling expectation equals its estimand under the stated model and sampling process.
major_error_concepts: Claiming an unbiased estimator must return the true parameter in each realized sample.

cards.prompt: Define uncertainty statement. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A qualified statement that names the estimand and estimate, interval or standard error, population and sampling scope, assumptions, and important uncertainty not captured numerically.
required_concepts: The statement names the estimand and the reported estimate.
The statement reports a confidence interval or standard error.
The statement identifies the population and sampling scope.
The statement states the assumptions that support the numerical uncertainty.
The statement identifies important uncertainty that the interval or standard error does not capture.
major_error_concepts: Presenting an interval without its estimand, population, procedure, assumptions, or limitations and calling uncertainty fully reported.

cards.prompt: Define variable. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A measured, assigned, or derived attribute whose possible values are defined for observational units.
required_concepts: A measured, assigned, or derived attribute whose possible values are defined for observational units.
major_error_concepts: Calling an unlabeled column a well-defined variable without specifying its units, coding, and observational meaning.

cards.prompt: State a two-sided z confidence interval for a mean, distinguishing exact normal-model coverage from approximation.
cards.definition: For n iid N(mu,sigma²) observations with known sigma>0, a two-sided 1-alpha confidence interval for mu is xbar ± z_(1-alpha/2) sigma/sqrt(n), where 0<alpha<1 and z_q is the standard-normal q quantile. The same expression can be used as an approximation under an appropriate sampling limit, but known variance alone does not make a nonnormal finite sample exactly normal.
required_concepts: Use xbar ± z_(1-alpha/2) sigma/sqrt(n).
The population standard deviation sigma is known.
Iid normal sampling gives exact coverage; other uses require an approximation argument.
major_error_concepts: Knowing the population variance makes this interval exact for any one-observation distribution.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Applied Statistics I.
